tagline.text: The last village of century-old Kalinga traditional tattooing

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱2,000–4,000 per person (per day, tattoo cost separate)

image.credit: Gubernatoria / CC BY 2.5 au / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: A Butbut village set above rice terraces deep in the Kalinga mountains, the hometown of the legendary traditional tattooist Apo Whang-od. You can get the traditional tattoo "batok," etched with bamboo and thorns, and experience Cordillera indigenous life up close at a mountain homestay.
Buscalan is a village terraced into a mountainside in Tinglayan, Kalinga, at about

above sea level, layered together with the surrounding rice terraces. Rugged mountains ring it across the Chico River valley, cutting it off from the outside world for a long time, and Kalinga's own culture remains correspondingly strong here. What has made this village known across the Philippines, and now the world, is the traditional tattoo "batok."

Kalinga batok was originally a mark of honor tattooed on warriors who defended the tribe, and for women it was a symbol of beauty and maturity. Ink made from charcoal powder mixed with water is applied to the skin using a pomelo (a grapefruit-family fruit) thorn, then tapped in with a bamboo stick. It takes longer and hurts more than a machine tattoo, but each design carries meaning drawn from nature and daily life, such as snakes, centipedes, eagles, and rice paddies.
The symbol of this tradition is Apo Whang-od Oggay, said to have been born in

. Once called "the last Kalinga tattooist," she has passed her skills on to her grandnieces Grace Palicas and Ilyang Wigan, among others, and dozens of young tattooists in the village now carry batok forward. In
, at over a hundred years old, she made headlines by appearing on the cover of Vogue Philippines.

The journey is long and rough and the facilities are basic, but if you visit with respect for a living indigenous culture, this is a place that can leave the deepest impression of any trip to the Philippines. It's recommended not only for travelers interested in tattoos, but also for those wanting a rice-terrace trek and a mountain homestay.
Village tattooists hand-etch the traditional design of your choice. A small design takes around
30 minutes
, while covering a whole arm can take several days, and prices range from hundreds to thousands of pesos depending on size and design.
Now elderly, Apo Whang-od gives her signature "three dots" tattoo instead of her signature design (about
). Whether and when she works varies with her health and village circumstances, so check locally through your guide.

blocks.title: Entering the village over the new suspension bridge

children.text: A new path crossing a suspension bridge over the valley from the end of the road now leads into the village, cutting the walk down to about
10–15 minutes
. The view of the rice terraces and village from the bridge is stunning.

blocks.title: Buscalan rice terrace and waterfall trek

children.text: Walk the paddy walls around the village to enjoy the mountain scenery, and with a guide you can also visit a nearby waterfall.
Stay in a resident's home, eat Kalinga home cooking, and chat with locals in the evening. You get a glimpse of village daily life that a day trip can't offer.
Kalinga is one of the Philippines' leading coffee-growing regions. Be sure to try the strong local coffee brewed at your homestay, and buying beans to take home is a good idea too.

During the rainy season,
June–October

, rain is frequent, and the Bontoc–Tinglayan mountain road is often closed by landslides. Roads can stay blocked for several days after a typhoon, so allow plenty of extra time in your schedule during this period. Keep in mind, too, that a tattoo getting wet in the rain can slow its healing.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary depending on local conditions.
Buscalan has no hotels; a homestay in a resident's home is the only accommodation. Your guide usually arranges it, at about

per person per night. Rooms with mats on the floor shared among several guests are typical, with a shared bathroom and cold showers as standard. Amenities are limited, but staying in a resident's living space is itself the heart of this trip. If you'd rather have more comfort, you can also visit as a day trip and stay in Bontoc or Sagada instead.

Meals at the homestay are simple: rice, vegetables, and chicken or pork dishes. Traditional Kalinga food includes smoked pork dishes and wild vegetable soup, and the region's coffee is popular for its strong aroma. Small shops in the village sell only snacks and drinks, so prepare any favorite snacks or needed items in Bontoc beforehand.
A guide is mandatory. Guides are village residents who also arrange your homestay and place in the tattoo queue, so it's convenient to contact one before you set out.
There are almost no ATMs between Buscalan and Bontoc. Bring plenty of cash for transport, accommodation, guide, and tattoo costs.
If you plan to get a tattoo, avoid drinking the day before, and afterward keep the area clean and avoid long exposure to sun and water. It helps to bring a moisturizing ointment.
Phone signal is only weakly available in parts of the village. Let your family know your schedule in advance, and download an offline map.
Bring a headlamp, a portable battery, personal toiletries, a towel, and a warm outer layer. Nights and dawns are colder than you'd expect.
The village has many sloped stone steps and dirt paths, so sneakers or trekking sandals are essential.
The tattoo queue starts forming at dawn. If you have a particular tattooist in mind, register your place through your guide as soon as you arrive.

Buscalan is a living village, not a tourist attraction. Always ask permission before photographing residents, including Apo Whang-od, and refrain from pushy photo requests or intruding into private spaces.
There's a risk of infection after getting a tattoo. Check hygiene conditions yourself, and think carefully if you have a skin condition or blood-related illness.
Some traditional designs carry special meaning within the community, so don't insist on a design your tattooist doesn't recommend.
Landslides are frequent on the Bontoc–Tinglayan road during the rainy season. Check road conditions before traveling and plan to arrive before dark.
Drinking and late-night noise in the village disturb residents' daily life. Follow the village rules your guide explains.
Carry all your trash back out. This mountain village lacks waste disposal facilities.
